en: The teaching that brings salvation has its fundamental principle; faith in the teaching can assist its practice. The practice of the manifest teaching accords with principle;
verified practice may be transmitted and propagated. What is it that practice propagates? It cannot be established without the various teachings.

What is it that the teachings assist? Nothing but wondrous practice can explain them. Thus, through gradual hearing of the three, one fully unifies the teachings and practices into a single path. If...

Consulting oral instructions to resolve essential points; establishing evidence to resolve doubts; drawing analogies to discern and choose; citing the extensive to resolve the concise; subsuming the broad to resolve the correct; resolving the flow of the commentary’s phrasing; resolving the path of comprehensive contemplation; judging errors according to the text; and determining fallacies by reference to the specific section.
Having grasped these various essential points, I have composed this preface to briefly set forth what has been transmitted, so as not to neglect the insights of my predecessors.
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Zhànruǎn of Bīlíng during the Táng dynasty. Question: [The text begins with a question.]
For what reason and by what causal conditions have you suddenly compiled this record?
Answer: Because there was no other alternative.
In recounting this causal origin, there are ten general purposes.
First, it is so that one may know there is a lineage of masters and not follow the arbitrary whims of one's own mind or those of heterodox teachers.
Second, it is for the sake of those who once followed a master but have abandoned the fundamental teachings to follow what they have not yet seen.
Third, it is to prevent future generations from developing successive divergent interpretations that would cause them to lose their original basis.
Fourth, it is for those who believe in this school but prefer to study elsewhere, so that they may have a teacher to receive and follow when no such teacher is available there.
Fifth, it is for the purpose of practicing the contemplation of meaning together with the teachings, so that those who rely on the scriptures may possess both practice and understanding.
Sixth, it is for the purpose of pointing out the joints and articulations, as well as the broad and concise passages, the beginnings and endings, and the essential tenets of the text.
Seventh, it is for the purpose of establishing the teacher’s understanding so that it does not fall into decline, thereby benefiting future generations.
Eighth, it is for the purpose of providing oneself with the means to examine one’s own understanding, thereby preventing errors and facilitating investigation.
Ninth, it is to reveal what has been understood, fearing that there may be confusion or forgetfulness, and thus seeking to eliminate errors through revision.
Tenth, it is to accord with the Buddha’s intent, mobilizing the mind of great compassion to perform deeds for the benefit of others.
This one section consists of three versions in total.
The first version comprises twenty fascicles,
while the second version comprises ten fascicles.
The title at the beginning of both versions is designated as "Perfect and Sudden" (yuantun) in order to distinguish it from the partial, the small, and the indeterminate teachings.
The second version is that in which the phrase "I humbly reflect" (qienian) appears at the beginning of the text.
The title of the third version differs slightly in its intended meaning, as will be fully explained in the commentary below;
it begins with the words: "Cessation and contemplation, clarity and stillness."
The version currently received is precisely the third edition.
At that time, people transmitted it such that they generally regarded the third as the abridged version and designated the second edition as the extensive version.
At first glance, it appears that there are differences in length;
however, upon examining the beginning and end, the number of pages is actually equal.
Therefore, the third version should be regarded as the re-edited original, and it need not be described as "abbreviated."
I have occasionally consulted and resolved my inquiries during audiences,
and have further augmented them through investigation and deliberation upon the sūtras and śāstras;
this is not a hasty composition based on mere personal opinion or erroneous assertions.
According to the commentaries on the sūtras and śāstras,
all [expositions] are divided into three sections;
yet even the current text’s formal exposition is not yet complete.
It is clear that there is no third section for circulation [of the text].
Only the portion preceding the opening chapter, where Zhiyan attached the preface, may be considered the introductory section (nidāna-bhāga).
From the beginning of the opening chapter onward constitutes the main exposition (samyag-deśanā-bhāga).
The second edition of the old version combined the preface and the main text into ten chapters;
therefore, the beginning of the text states: "I humbly reflect that the accounts of what I have heard together constitute ten points.
The term "humbly reflect" (qièniàn) means to privately and secretly give rise to a thought.
The preface has five points:
first, a general overview;
second, the lineage of patriarchal succession.
Third, distinguishing the differences;
fourth, citing evidence;
fifth, indicating the locations.
The term "narrating what has been heard" (*śrutam-anuśamsati*) refers to recording that which one has received.
The formal exposition also consists of five intentions.
First, the opening of the chapter.
First, arising; second, differentiation;
third, detailed analysis.
Fifth, regarding the explanation:
combining the preface with the section on what was heard to form ten sections seems somewhat unstable in its intent;
therefore, it has been revised and finalized by omitting this sequence so that only the Preface and the Main Body are established.
Furthermore, regarding the fact that only the "initiation" (*samutthāna*) and so forth are presented in the introduction without an expression of homage,
this is because the merit is attributed solely to the Master’s *Vyākhyāyukti* (Explanatory Commentary).
If one follows the actual text of the Great Master’s exposition, the meaning can be divided into three sections.
Thus, the preceding six sections constitute the introductory division (*nidāna-vibhāga*);
the correct contemplation of the fruits and retributions constitutes the main body (*mūla-bhāga*);
and the arousal of the teaching for the sake of transforming others constitutes the dissemination division (*paryavasāna-vibhāga*).
Since the ultimate aim is the cessation of transformation and the return to quiescence,
its meaning seems to transcend the three [trainings] as they are conventionally categorized; yet,
in the commentary (*śāstra*), even when discussing practice, it is still structured into three parts in relation to the three trainings.
Now, why would it not be permissible to follow that same principle and open up three sections?
For now, let us rely on the previous two sections as the primary structure;
to the initial introduction, we shall add details such as the time and place where [the teaching] was heard to constitute the "General Introduction" (sūtra-nidāna).
The use of the "Old Preface," "Succession of Patriarchs," "Human Dharma," and other such matters constitutes the separate preface;
this is precisely the intention for re-editing and determining [the text].
One must not again employ the "Discussions" and the other five [sections].
Considering that the text concerning the sequence, the divisions, and the repeated treatment of time, place, and so forth has been reorganized,
I have therefore revised the previous provisional analysis to establish it as a complete realization.
Thus, the subsequent section employs this revised analytical text, stating:
Now, based on the sutras, I shall further clarify the Perfect and Sudden [teaching].

Regarding the phrase "based on the sutras," this refers precisely to citing scriptural evidence; having finished proving the Perfect and Sudden, I now request that you provide proof for the remaining two [teachings].
He then posed the question:
"I wish to hear the authentic testimony regarding the other samādhis.
This question is omitted from the second version.
Therefore, the second version’s "Brief Summary" (Shānglüe) states:
"Briefly citing Buddhist scriptures to roughly manifest the intent of the Perfect [Teaching].
Thus, one should know that the "Brief Summary" is not different from the "Citing of Evidence."
Therefore, I have revised the section on "investigating and determining" (*samlakṣaṇa-viniścaya*) by changing the term "investigating" (*samlakṣaṇa*) to "citing evidence" (*āgamopanyāsa*).

If one were to apply the sequence of terms such as "investigating and determining" from the previous version to correspond with the text of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* itself, [the order would be as follows].
In that case, passages such as "stopping and contemplation are clear and still" would be rendered superfluous;
moreover, it is highly inappropriate to attempt to evaluate [the teachings] in opposition to the ancestral transmission.
Therefore, one must discard the sequential order of the old chapters.

Now, in revising and finalizing this work with the addition of the general preface, I have intended to categorize it according to the five topics—such as the essence of the Dharma—as recorded in the accounts of the First Council;
therefore, it differs from previous versions that placed the "Brief Survey" at the beginning.
Having already described the sequence of the presence or absence of the new and old [versions],
there are two reasons why the name was changed to *Mahā*:
first, to distinguish it from the "Minor" (*kṣudra*) *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* produced by his lay elder brother.
Second, it is for the purpose of preserving the Sanskrit sounds while simultaneously encompassing their rich semantic content.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The term *mahā* contains three meanings."
This refers to "much," "great," and "superior.
The explanation of the stage of a bhikṣu based on the four teachings in the *Shu* (Commentary) does not accord with the present intent.
Using these three names to explain the three contemplations of the Perfect [Teaching] is precisely what accords with the purpose of the title.
"Great" (Mahā) signifies emptiness (śūnyatā); "Much" (Bahu) signifies the provisional (prajñapti); and "Supreme" (Agra) signifies the middle (madhyama).
Therefore, the title is revised to adopt a name that encompasses all these meanings, thereby designating this section as "The Single Mind and Threefold Contemplation."
If that is so, what is the difference [between this] and the Complete and Sudden [teaching], which has shifted toward the Mahāyāna? Answer:
Although the names "Perfect and Sudden" differ from "Partial and Gradual," their terminology is general and lacks the inclusion of the three [vehicles]. Therefore,
the single and shallow sounds of this land have been revised to preserve the polysemous designations of that [scripture].
By this, one should know that the two characters "Cessation" (śamatha) and "Contemplation" (vipaśyanā) are none other than Mahā;
they are precisely the cessation and contemplation of the single mind’s three cessations and three contemplations.
Thus, it is known that the entire treatise is subsumed within these as its primary title.
From the "General Meaning" at the beginning to the "Ultimate Aim" at the end, there is nothing that is not the *mahāyāna* śamatha-vipaśyanā.
Thus, while the title serves as the general heading for the ten chapters,
within those ten chapters, the "General Meaning" itself is the general part and the remaining eight are the specific parts.

Thus, one knows that both the general and specific aspects of the causes and effects of one's own practice, as well as the capacities for transforming others and being transformed by them, are all the Mahā-Excellence of Samādhi and Prajñā. Why is this?
Within the general explanation, the arousal of the bodhicitta and the cultivation of practice constitute the causes of one's own practice.
Next, one experiences the great fruit, which is the fruition of one's own practice.
Next, one tears asunder the great net, which is the ability to transform others.
Since there is the capacity to transform, there must necessarily be those who are transformed.
The text briefly cites the "capable" (the means) to encompass the "object" (the goal).
Once the matters of the capable and the object are concluded, they together enter the ultimate destination.
Within the detailed explanation, from the initial definition of names up to the correct contemplation, these constitute the causes for one's own practice.
The "Chapter on Retribution" concerns the fruit of one's own practice;
the "Chapter on Initiating the Teaching" concerns the capacity for transforming others;
and the meaning of "that which is received" corresponds to the locus of transforming others.

The final three major chapters are deficient in their textual detail; since their meaning and intent are identical to the latter three sections within the "General" [section], the subsequent text is abbreviated and not explained.

Although the general introduction (*nidāna*) typically compiles the five common elements of a sutra, since this is a private record,

Within this [introduction], there are six parts.
The first four characters describe the essence of what was heard;
the two characters "stopping" (śamatha) and "contemplation" (vipaśyanā) correctly indicate the essence of that which was heard;
and the two characters "clarity" and "tranquility" praise the virtues of that essence.
This means that the essence of *śamatha* (calm abiding) is stillness, while the essence of *vipaśyanā* (insight) is clarity.

Throughout the ten chapters from beginning to end, the ten dharmas of correct contemplation are none other than the essence of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, wherein both stillness and clarity are fully manifest.
